title: Guelph Innovation District development deferred over industrial compatibility
subtitle: Also: winter maintenance audit, Ontario Land Tribunal advocacy, Wyndham Street streetscape review and a downtown board appointment.
overview: Council's main item was the Guelph Innovation District, Blocks 1 and 2, a proposal for roughly 4,700 homes. Council approved the part of the Official Plan amendment that staff supported. It deferred the rest, including the zoning and subdivision applications, until the applicant provides the required land use compatibility studies. Staff must report back within 60 days of receiving that information, and staff and the developer were directed to keep working together. Staff had recommended refusing those applications because nearby industry, including a large beef processing plant, could be affected by odour, noise and air emissions. Council approved both motions {{vote:m6}} {{vote:m7}}.

Council also accepted a winter maintenance audit and put its recommendations ahead of a wider service-level review {{vote:m8}}. It asked the Province to review the Ontario Land Tribunal {{vote:m9}}. It directed staff to review the new Wyndham Street streetscape against the earlier design and report in early 2027 {{vote:m10}}. It also appointed a member to the downtown business association board {{vote:m2}}.

After a closed session, the mayor reported that Council gave staff direction on a Gordon Street Ontario Land Tribunal matter and received information on an organizational structure review. This was Council's last decision meeting before the fall election for several members.

decisions.detail: Council approved Official Plan Amendment No. 115 and deferred the remaining official plan, zoning and subdivision components until the required information is submitted, with a staff report due within 60 days of receiving it {{vote:m6}}.
Council directed staff and the developer to keep working together on outstanding matters, including land use compatibility {{vote:m7}}.
Council received the audit, directed staff to prioritize its recommendations and report back after winter 2026/2027, and deferred the operational review until then {{vote:m8}}.

Council asked the Province to review the tribunal's role, strengthen deference to evidence-based municipal planning decisions and reduce municipal defence costs, and to circulate the resolution widely {{vote:m9}}.
Staff will review options to bring the east side of Wyndham Street closer to the 90% design while protecting the new area, and identify material design differences, reporting in Q1 2027 {{vote:m10}}.
Council approved capital budget reallocations, including a net-zero shift of $600,000 to the cast iron water main replacement program from the Ontario Street reconstruction project.
Council appointed Denise Mansur to the association's board for a term ending November 2026 or until a successor is appointed {{vote:m2}}.

debate: Agricultural groups and the processing company said the beef plant is critical, hard-to-replace infrastructure. They worried that nearby homes would bring complaints and operating limits. They asked Council to reject or defer the applications until odour, air and noise studies are done.

Staff and an independent peer reviewer said compatibility has not been shown. They said that once land is zoned for homes, the cost of any needed mitigation falls on existing industry, which cannot appeal later steps. They said this is why conditions or holding provisions could not fix the gap.

The developer and its consultants said the approved block plan keeps homes 300 metres from the plant and that compatibility is achievable. They said studies were under way but needed data from industry and freedom-of-information requests. They asked for approval with conditions, or at least a firm timeline and early draft conditions.

Councillors asked why the developer could not simply commit to paying for all mitigation and how long the studies would take. Staff and the peer reviewer said the timeline depends on data and possible field work. Several councillors urged both sides to meet and share information, and a meeting was scheduled for that week.

On winter maintenance, one councillor said the audit's findings did not match residents' experience of icy east-end streets last winter. Staff cited a salt delivery shortage, the provincial minimum standards and the move to in-house residential plowing. They said route changes and better notifications could start this winter, but equipment purchases would need budget approval.
